extracted.intended_audience: general readers of satirical counsel on marriage (readers of Rabelaisian humor)
extracted.subtask_description: A comic, dialogued set of counsels (theologue, physician, philosopher, lawyer) on whether Panurge should marry and on ways to prevent cuckoldry or control concupiscence. Mixes practical prescriptions, medical folklore, and moral/religious guidance in a humorous early-modern voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult with yourself about bodily desire
rubrics_metrics.description: Before seeking external counsel, examine your own state: 'Do you find any trouble or disquiet in your body by the importunate stings and pricklings of the flesh?' and whether you possess the gift of continency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hippothadee insists one must first 'consult with yourself' and assess carnal impulses; the presence or absence of continency (self-control) is central to the marriage decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marry if you cannot practice continency
rubrics_metrics.description: If you lack the 'gift and special grace of continency' and burn with concupiscence, it is better to marry than to continue suffering desire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hippothadee's explicit counsel: 'my counsel to you in that case ... is that you marry; for you should rather choose to marry once than to burn still in fires of concupiscence.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a wife of commendable extraction and piety
rubrics_metrics.description: Select a bride 'of a commendable extraction, descended of honest parents, and instructed in all piety and virtue' who has not frequented corrupt company and loves and fears God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hippothadee argues that such a woman, fearing God and educated in virtue, will be unlikely to commit adultery; lineage, upbringing, piety, and virtuous associations are listed as safeguards against cuckoldry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Husband must set a public, exemplary moral example
rubrics_metrics.description: The husband should behave so as to be a model of conjugal amity and visible virtue—'go before her in a good example' and live devoutly and chastely 'in the face also of all men and open view of the world.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theologue stresses that a husband's conduct trains his wife toward fidelity; the moon/sun analogy is used to explain how the husband's virtue enlightens the wife.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek multidisciplinary counsel for a complex personal question
rubrics_metrics.description: Enlist a theologian for spiritual matters, a physician for bodily concerns, a lawyer for goods, and a philosopher for broader resolution: each 'is appointed for the soul, the body, and the goods.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pantagruel's plan is to convene a divine, a physician, a lawyer, and a philosopher to examine Panurge's perplexity from complementary perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of philauty (self-love) biasing your decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-love (philauty) blinds judgment; one should be aware that personal affection or selfish interest may distort the assessment of whether to marry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pantagruel explicitly warns that philauty deceiveth and blinds the judgment in such personal determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep busy—frequent labour abates lust
rubrics_metrics.description: Continual toil and painful exercises reduce the ardour of lechery by dissipating bodily resources and spirits necessary for sexual desire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rondibilis (via ancient authorities) presents labour as a prophylactic: soldiers, hunters, and constantly occupied people are less susceptible to venereal appetite; idleness is called 'the mother of luxury.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Eager study distracts and blunts sexual appetite
rubrics_metrics.description: Deep, earnest intellectual study channels the vital spirits into the mind, leaving insufficient impetus for venereal desire—scholars and Muses are cited as examples of chastity preserved by study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rondibilis and literary examples (Democritus, Socrates, the Muses) argue that contemplative absorption suspends natural faculties and so subdues lechery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use intoxicants or specific drugs/herbs to suppress libido (with caveats)
rubrics_metrics.description: Immoderate wine and certain plants/herbs (e.g., water-lily, agnus castus, chaste tree, mandrake, hemp) are reported to cool or benumb the generative faculty and so reduce lust; conversely, moderate wine can stimulate desire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rondibilis distinguishes dose and effect: excessive drinking causes numbness and impotence, while moderate drinking excites; a long list of substances is given as purported anti-libidinal remedies, with the implicit medical/folkloric framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequent sexual reiteration (maceration) diminishes ardour
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated indulgence in venery ('maceration and taming of the flesh')—having sex often—will, according to some, tame and bring down the pride of the body and depress sensual desire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters cite hermits and priors who recommend frequent acts (twenty-five or thirty times a day, humorously) as a method to mortify the flesh; this is presented as one of five bodily strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical constitution, temperament, and age affect marriage fitness
rubrics_metrics.description: A man's bodily make, humoral temperament, complexion, and age determine his suitability for marriage; Rondibilis describes Panurge as 'neatly featured... of a good temperament... of a competent age... forward mind to be married.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Medical/physiological assessment is used as a criterion for readiness to marry: constitution and humours matter in the physician's judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use physical tokens or contrivances against cuckoldry (Hans Carvel’s ring)
rubrics_metrics.description: Story of Hans Carvel's ring: wearing a ring said to reveal/ensure that a wife will not be known carnally by another without the husband's knowledge is presented as an 'infallible and sovereign antidote' to cuckoldry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tale is given as a comic, folkloric 'expedient'—an object-based prophylactic against infidelity; presented humorously rather than as sober counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame undertakings with deference to God's will ('if it please God')
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefacing decisions with the clause 'If it please God' is canonical and proper to acknowledge divine providence and humility in human undertakings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hippothadee defends using the conditional as a sanctifying, pious habit that recognizes dependence on God's will when resolving human doubts (including about marriage).
